headline: Argentina presses its claim to the Falkland Islands

sources.title: Argentina's Milei steps up Falklands sovereignty claims with oil sanctions (Reuters via Investing.com)
Argentina escalates Falklands dispute with the U.K., seizing on Trump comments (AP via NPR)
Argentina's Milei threatens sanctions as he refocuses on Falklands (Al Jazeera)
Argentina's Milei escalates Falklands dispute in sovereignty push against Britain (video, FRANCE 24 English)

chunks.text: On September 3, 2026, Argentine President Javier Milei {{stepped up}} his country's claim to the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, in a [[nationally televised address]]. He said he would {{speed up}} [[sanctions]] against companies working on the Sea Lion [[offshore]] oil project, about 220 kilometers north of the islands, and {{go after}} their [[suppliers]], [[shareholders]], and directors. He also promised extra funding for a [[naval base]] in the far south of Argentina.

verbs.correct: To increase the force of something
verbs.wrong: To leave a top political job
verbs.why: A city steps up security before a big game, and a store steps up its advertising before the holidays. On September 3, 2026, President Javier Milei stepped up Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands in a nationally televised address.

verbs.wrong: To put something to a vote
verbs.why: A new road can speed up the trip to the airport, and a second cook speeds up service in a busy restaurant. Milei said he would speed up sanctions against companies working on the Sea Lion oil project.

verbs.correct: To try to punish or catch someone
verbs.wrong: To agree to support a plan
verbs.why: Police go after the people who plan a robbery, and a tax office goes after companies that hide income. Milei said Argentina would also go after the project's suppliers, shareholders, and directors.

chunks.text: Milei said he would send Congress a [[bill]] to {{crack down on}} [[unauthorized]] activity near the islands and {{shut out}} the companies involved from doing business in Argentina. "Argentina will not stand idly by," he said, calling any further advance there a threat to [[national security]]. A British company and an Israeli company, which run Sea Lion, plan to {{press ahead}} with drilling this year and {{pump out}} oil from 2028. The British firm's shares fell 6 percent, but both say their [[licenses]] are valid.

verbs.wrong: To surrender a claim to land
verbs.why: A city can crack down on illegal parking, and a school can crack down on cheating during exams. Milei said he would send Congress a bill to crack down on unauthorized activity near the islands.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from taking part
verbs.wrong: To close a business for good
verbs.why: A club can shut out members who do not pay, and a country can shut out foreign banks from its market. The bill would shut out the companies involved in the oil project from doing business in Argentina.

verbs.correct: To continue with a plan anyway
verbs.why: A builder presses ahead with a project despite the rain, and a student presses ahead with her studies after a bad grade. The British and Israeli companies plan to press ahead with drilling this year.

verbs.correct: To produce large amounts of something
verbs.wrong: To ship oil to another country
verbs.why: A factory pumps out thousands of shoes a day, and a small studio can pump out a new song every week. The companies hope to pump out oil from the Sea Lion field from 2028.

chunks.text: Britain {{hit back}} quickly. Britain's [[defense secretary]] said the islands are British because the islanders choose to be British, and Britain's [[commitment]] to them is "absolute and unshakeable." Britain's foreign secretary said the islanders' right to [[self-determination]] is [[paramount]]. Britain {{backs up}} its position with a 2013 [[referendum]], when about 4,000 islanders voted [[overwhelmingly]] to remain a British [[overseas territory]]. The defense secretary {{played down}} the speech as "domestic politics in Argentina."

verbs.correct: To reply strongly to an attack
verbs.why: A singer hits back at critics on social media, and a coach hits back when reporters question his team. Britain hit back quickly after Milei's address, saying the islands are British.

verbs.wrong: To hold a public vote on something
verbs.why: A lawyer backs up her case with documents, and a scientist backs up a claim with data. Britain backs up its position with a 2013 referendum in which about 4,000 islanders voted to stay British.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To pretend to agree with someone
verbs.why: A company plays down a small data leak, and a runner plays down an injury before a race. Britain's defense secretary played down Milei's speech, saying it reflected domestic politics in Argentina.

chunks.text: The dispute {{dates back}} decades. A 74-day war in 1982 killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British [[service members]], and three islanders. Milei also {{brought up}} U.S. President Donald Trump's comment on August 31 that he was reviewing the [[neutral]] U.S. position. [[Opposition lawmakers]] accused Milei of using the issue to {{shore up}} support before next year's election. Neither government has {{backed down}}, but Argentina has not announced any [[military operation]].

verbs.correct: To have started at a past time
verbs.wrong: To end after a fixed period
verbs.why: The old church dates back to the 1600s, and their friendship dates back to college. The dispute over the islands dates back decades, to the 1982 war and before.
A worker brings up the question of pay at a meeting, and a friend brings up an old story at dinner. Milei brought up a recent comment by U.S. President Donald Trump in his address.

verbs.wrong: To send more troops to an area
verbs.why: A bank shores up its finances by selling assets, and a coach shores up the defense with a new player. Opposition lawmakers accused Milei of using the issue to shore up support before next year's election.

verbs.correct: To withdraw a claim or demand
verbs.wrong: To return to an earlier plan
verbs.why: A union backs down after the company offers a small raise, and a shopper backs down after the manager shows him the store's return policy. Neither government has backed down, but Argentina has not announced any military operation.

mainIdea.s: Argentina's president promised sanctions on a Falklands oil project and money for a naval base to press his claim. Britain replied that the islands are British by the islanders' own choice.
mainIdea.why: Argentina announced sanctions on the Sea Lion project and funding for a naval base in the far south of Argentina, and Britain said its commitment to the islands is absolute and unshakeable.

mainIdea.s: Argentina's president threatened oil companies near the Falklands with sanctions and promised a bigger navy presence. Britain agreed to open talks on sharing the oil found near the islands.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Britain did not offer talks. It said the islands are British because the islanders choose to be British, and that its commitment to them is absolute and unshakeable.

mainIdea.s: Britain and Argentina signed a deal to restore direct flights to the islands and share fishing data. Officials on both sides called it a small but real first step toward better relations.
mainIdea.why: There was no deal on flights or fishing. Argentina announced sanctions and naval funding, and Britain restated that sovereignty rests with the U.K.

tf.s: Milei stepped up Argentina's claim to the islands in a televised address.
tf.why: On September 3, 2026, he made a nationally televised address and promised extra funding for a naval base in the far south of Argentina.

tf.s: The Sea Lion oil project lies about 220 kilometers south of the islands.
tf.why: Sea Lion lies about 220 kilometers north of the islands, and its two operators plan to pump out oil from 2028.

tf.s: Britain's defense secretary played down the speech as domestic politics.
tf.why: Britain hit back quickly, and the defense secretary called Milei's speech domestic politics in Argentina while calling Britain's commitment to the islands absolute and unshakeable.

tf.s: The 1982 war between Argentina and Britain lasted about two years.
tf.why: The dispute dates back decades, and the 1982 war lasted 74 days, killing 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members, and three islanders.

tf.s: About 4,000 islanders voted in 2013 to remain a British overseas territory.
tf.why: Britain backs up its position with the 2013 referendum, in which the islanders voted overwhelmingly to stay British.

tf.s: Argentina has backed down from its claim to the islands.
tf.why: Neither government has backed down, but Argentina has not announced any military operation.

lines.text: Did you see that Argentina's president {{stepped up}} the Falklands claim again?
The Malvinas speech? I caught part of it. [[Here we go again]].
This time it's about oil. There's a project called Sea Lion, about 220 kilometers north of the islands, and he wants to {{speed up}} sanctions against the companies working on it.
No, he said he would {{go after}} their suppliers, shareholders, and directors too. And he's sending Congress a bill to {{crack down on}} anything unauthorized near the islands.
So the idea is to {{shut out}} anyone who touches that project from doing business in Argentina.
Exactly. Plus extra funding for a naval base in the far south of Argentina.
And the companies? Are they still going to drill?
They say their licenses are valid and they'll {{press ahead}}. Drilling this year, and they hope to {{pump out}} oil from 2028.
They {{hit back}} the same day. Britain's defense secretary said the islands are British because the islanders choose to be British, and that Britain's commitment is absolute and unshakeable.
[[That's the sticking point]], isn't it? Argentina talks about sovereignty, Britain talks about what the islanders want.
Right. Britain {{backs up}} its position with the 2013 referendum, when about 4,000 islanders voted to stay British. Their defense secretary {{played down}} the whole speech as domestic politics.
Well, there's an election in Argentina next year. [[Timing is everything]].
The opposition said the same thing. They think he's using the issue to {{shore up}} support.
Is anyone worried about another war? That one in 1982 was terrible.
Nobody has {{backed down}}, but Argentina hasn't announced any military operation. [[So far it's just words]], at least for now.

expressions.def: Used when something unwelcome is happening one more time and you are tired of it
ex: The train is late? Here we go again.
They're arguing about the budget. Here we go again.

expressions.def: Used to name the one issue that stops two sides from agreeing
ex: They agree on the price, but the delivery date is the sticking point.
Who pays for repairs? That's the sticking point in the contract.

expressions.def: Used to say that when something happens matters as much as what happens
ex: She asked for a raise right after the big sale. Timing is everything.
He launched the app the week before the holidays. Timing is everything.

expressions.def: Used to say that a threat or promise has not yet been followed by any real action
ex: The mayor promised to fight the plan, but so far it's just words.
They keep saying they'll sue. So far it's just words.

expressions.expr: Let's hope it stays that way
expressions.def: Used to say you want a good or calm situation to continue
ex: No accidents on the site this year. Let's hope it stays that way.
The baby finally sleeps all night. Let's hope it stays that way.
